title: stage-telemetry-interaction-map-notes
content:
Purpose:
This is a working set of notes and lightweight analysis for building an interaction map of per-stage telemetry across e2e traces. The goal is to move beyond isolated per-stage percentiles and capture cross-stage dependencies that explain weird p95/p99 behavior for specific cohorts (seqlen buckets, kv-miss vs kv-hit, cold vs warm workers).

Background / Why: 
We have a lot of good single-stage breakdowns but they often fail to explain tail coupling: e.g., p99 spikes where emit looks normal but upstream batching/wait states or egress stalls amplify the tail. The interaction map is an adjacency-like view: each stage -> stage edge contains correlation metrics (lag, conditional p95 increase, percent of traces where downstream stage amplifies).

Quick hypothesis inventory (prioritized):
1) Async-batcher handoff latency correlates with p99 when batch sizes are low but concurrency is high (observed on smaller models + short prompts).
2) KV-cache miss spikes show >2x p95 increase in the attention-compile stage due to decoder kernel fallbacks and memory touch patterns.
3) Egress serialization (json + instrumentation overhead) occasionally dominates p99 for requests with large structured outputs (function calling), but only when token emission is bursty.

Data slice definitions used in this draft: 
- Cohorts: seqlen: [<=64, 65-256, 257-1024]; kv: [hit, miss]; worker_warmth: [warm (>=10 reqs), cold (<10 reqs)]
- Percentiles reported: p50, p95, p99 for each stage and whole e2e
- Trace sample: 20k traces sampled over 24h (2024-10-15), stratified by route and model.

Key metrics we extract per trace (fields): 
- trace_id
- route
- model
- cohort tags (seqlen, kv, warm/cold)
- per-stage durations (tokenize, preprocess, batching_wait, compile, attention, kv_lookup, emit, egress)
- batch_size at time of request
- worker_id
- cpu/gpu_migrations (flag)
- any retry/fallback flags

Observations (raw):
- For seqlen <=64 and kv=hit: p95 e2e = 82ms, p99 = 240ms. The largest contributor to p99 is batching_wait (median 8ms but p99 160ms) and emit (p99 40ms).
- For seqlen 65-256 and kv=miss: p95 e2e = 210ms, p99 = 520ms. The attention stage median is 80ms but p99 300ms; compile stage shows p99 spike only on kv-miss traces.
- Cold workers increase e2e p99 by ~1.6x on average compared to warm; compile and attention have higher variance.

Interaction map snippets (verbal):
- batching_wait -> compile: When batching_wait > 50ms (rare), compile p99 tends to increase by +40-60ms. Interpretation: long wait implies small batches or scheduling jitter causing worker to choose a slower kernel path for compile.
- kv_lookup -> attention: kv-miss traces are strongly correlated with higher attention p99. There are two plausible reasons: (1) the attention implementation touches more memory pages on kv miss; (2) fallback quant kernels used for kv miss path are slower.
- emit -> egress: bursty emit patterns (many small writes) correlate to higher egress p99, suggesting our serialization path is sensitive to token-chunk patterns.

Case study (anomalous day 2024-10-09 02:00UTC):
- Route: chat-streaming-v2, model: rwd-small-3b, cohort: seqlen<=64, kv=hit
- Observed a p99 spike from 95ms baseline to 480ms for 30 minutes.
- Traces show: batching_wait p99 increased to 320ms; batch_size distribution shifted lower (more singleton batches); worker churn increased (OOM-kill events upstream).
- Root cause hypothesis: upstream node autoscaler induced worker restarts causing bursts of singleton batches hitting the async-batcher; handoff latency ballooned and amplified the tail.
- Remediations taken: temporarily bumped min-replicas for that pool; p99 returned to baseline after 12 minutes.

Quick stats table (text):
- Cohort: <=64/kv=hit: e2e p50/p95/p99 = 45ms / 82ms / 240ms
- Cohort: 65-256/kv=miss: e2e p50/p95/p99 = 120ms / 210ms / 520ms
- Cohort: 257+/kv=miss: e2e p50/p95/p99 = 540ms / 820ms / 1600ms
(These are sample numbers from the stratified trace set — not canonical benchmarks.)

Experimental analysis steps we want in the next round: 
- Build a simple adjacency matrix output per cohort where cell(i,j) = conditional increase in j.p95 when i.p95 > threshold. This will let us rank edges by amplification factor.
- Run a controlled microbenchmark: force singleton batches for 10k samples across seqlen buckets to measure batching_wait -> compile amplification directly.
- Add a lightweight flag in trace header for kernel-type (quant fallback vs optimized) so we can attribute attention spikes to kernel selection.

Suggested instrumentation tweaks (low cost):
- Emit batching metadata in the initial trace event: planned batch_size and actual batch_size and the worker selection timestamp. This makes handoff windows explicit.
- Record a kernel_tag enum in compile/attention events (fast-path|fallback|quantized) — small switch in the runtime that sets a tag string.

Unresolved questions / notes to self: 
- Is the compile spike on kv-miss consistent across GPUs or only specific instance types? Need mapping to instance-type labels.
- There are a handful of traces where emit latency is extreme (>500ms) but emit size is tiny — look for thread saturation or GC on user-land egress handler.
- Could client-side keepalive or slow consumer behavior be causing perceived egress p99? Need to correlate with downstream ack/transport metrics.

Action items (owners):
- Ethan: prototype adjacency matrix exporter (target: 2-week spike). Link: GH-PR skeleton in linked_artifacts.
- Lina: schedule microbenchmark for singleton batch forcing across three seqlen buckets (target: 1-week).
- Marcus: add kernel_tag to compile/attention traces and roll to staging (target: 3 days).
- Priya (me): synthesize a 1-pager for SRE/Autoscaler about observed worker-churn -> singleton batch tail amplification and propose a default min-replicas config (target: EOD Friday).

Quick TL;DR for on-call / SRE: 
- Tail amplification frequently arises not because one stage is slow in isolation, but because upstream scheduling/hand-off variance produces small batches or cold starts that cascade. Short-term mitigations: increase min-replicas for highly tail-sensitive routes, add a brief burst buffer for async-batcher, and instrument kernel tags to split attention tail sources.

Appendix (notes & scratch):
- Example trace snippet (condensed):
  trace: abc123 | seqlen 32 | batch_size 1 | batching_wait 220ms | compile 18ms | attention 45ms | emit 3ms | egress 2ms | worker_warmth=3
  observer: when batching_wait>200ms this trace was a p99 outlier; 70% of similar outliers share batch_size=1

- Quick grep pointers: look for earlier Slack thread: "trace-anomalies-2024-10" and GH issue serving-runtime/latency-523 which has preliminary query snippets (useful queries: join traces by worker_id and time-window, compute conditional percentiles).

End of notes. This doc will be iterated; it's intentionally conversational. Add your scratch findings below or push PRs to the adjacency exporter repo.
